title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
summary: Deep learning regression and classification tools typically do not capture model uncertainty, whereas Bayesian models do but at prohibitive computational cost. The paper casts dropout training in neural networks as approximate variational inference in deep Gaussian processes, yielding MC dropout: averaging T stochastic forward passes to estimate predictive mean and variance. On UCI regression benchmarks, notably Boston Housing, MC dropout improves test RMSE and predictive log-likelihood over VI and probabilistic back-propagation, achieving 2.97 ± 0.19 RMSE on Boston Housing in the 20-split setting.

claims.statement: MC dropout test RMSE on Boston Housing is 2.97 ± 0.19 (mean ± standard error over 20 random splits), outperforming PBP (3.01 ± 0.18) and VI (4.32 ± 0.29).

claims.config_for_value: Dropout NN with 1 hidden layer of 50 units, dropout probabilities 0.05 and 0.005, prior length-scale l=10^-2, tau found by 40-iteration Bayesian optimization on validation log-likelihood, then trained with 10x more epochs (400) using mini-batches of size 32 and Adam; MC dropout averages T stochastic forward passes.
claims.est_compute: CPU, ~1-3 min per split; ~30-60 min for 20 splits + BO

match_target.why: Boston Housing is the smallest dataset (N=506) in the target setting and shows the central result: MC dropout gives better RMSE than PBP and VI. It is the cheapest claim that still demonstrates the paper's main quantitative contribution.

tolerance.why: Table 1 reports ±0.19 standard error over 20 random splits for Boston Housing RMSE in the target Dropout configuration; this is the paper's reported spread for the target setting.

requirements.stmt: Use a neural network with one hidden layer of 50 units for the UCI regression benchmarks in Table 1.
requirements.quote: network size is very small (with 50 units following (Hern ́andez-Lobato & Adams, 2015))

requirements.stmt: Apply dropout before every weight layer with dropout probabilities 0.05 and 0.005.
requirements.quote: We used dropout with probabilities 0.05 and 0.005 since the network size is very small

requirements.stmt: Derive L2 weight decay from the model precision tau and prior length-scale l using eq. (7).
requirements.quote: the prior length-scale l and model precision τ are simply used to define the model’s weight decay through eq. (7).

requirements.stmt: Use Bayesian optimization (Spearmint) over validation log-likelihood to find optimal tau, with 40 BO iterations.
requirements.quote: we use Bayesian optimisation (BO, (Snoek et al., 2012; Snoek & authors, 2015)) over validation log-likelihood to find optimal τ

requirements.stmt: After BO, train the final model with 10x more iterations/epochs than BO's 40 (i.e., 400 epochs).
requirements.quote: after finding the optimal parameter values we used 10x more iterations, as dropout takes longer to converge

requirements.stmt: Use mini-batches of size 32 and the Adam optimizer.
requirements.quote: Finally, we used mini-batches of size 32 and the Adam optimiser (Kingma & Ba, 2014).

requirements.stmt: Set the prior length-scale to l = 10^-2 for most datasets based on the range of the data.
requirements.quote: set the prior length-scale to 10−2 for most datasets based on the range of the data.

requirements.stmt: At test time, use MC dropout: perform T stochastic forward passes and average predictions for RMSE (eq. 6).
requirements.quote: In practice this is equivalent to performing T stochastic forward passes through the network and averaging the results.

requirements.stmt: Evaluate predictive log-likelihood using the regression Monte Carlo approximation in eq. (8) when comparing to VI and PBP.
requirements.quote:
For regression this is given by:
log p(y∗|x∗, X, Y) ≈logsumexp

requirements.stmt: Average results over 20 random splits for Boston Housing and most datasets; use 5 splits for Protein Structure.
Use the UCI regression datasets with N and Q as in Table 1 and the same data preprocessing/splits as Hernandez-Lobato & Adams (2015).
requirements.quote: We replicate the experiment set-up in Hern ́andez-Lobato & Adams (2015)

requirements.stmt: Do not use early stopping; train for the fixed number of epochs determined by the BO + 10x schedule.
requirements.quote: after finding the optimal parameter values we used 10x more iterations, as dropout takes longer to converge

requirements.stmt: Implement with Keras and Theano backend, matching the paper's released code/demos.
requirements.quote: To implement the model we used Keras (Chollet, 2015), an open source deep learning package based on Theano (Bergstra et al., 2010).
